conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment process.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To get started, I need to ask you about the child (or children) you're claiming for.

**How old is your child?**

This is important because eligibility rules differ based on age:
- Children under 16 generally qualify automatically (with some conditions)
- Young people aged 16-19 may qualify if they're in approved education or training
- Those aged 20 or over don't usually qualify

Please tell me your child's age, and if you have multiple children you'd like to check eligibility for, please let me know about all of them.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm asking about my son Alex - he's 18 years old and lives at home with me.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you're asking about your son Alex who is 18 years old and lives at home with you.

Since Alex is 18 (which falls in the 16-19 age range), his eligibility will depend on whether he's in approved education or training.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Is Alex currently in approved education or training?**

For 16-19 year olds, you can claim Child Benefit if they are:
- In full-time non-advanced education (like A-levels, Scottish Highers, or similar qualifications), OR
- In approved unpaid training

Please let me know:
1. Is Alex currently studying or in training?
2. If he's not currently studying, has he recently left education (within the last few months)?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, Alex is currently studying. He's doing his A-levels at the local sixth form college.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! Alex is doing A-levels at sixth form college, which is exactly the type of education that can qualify for Child Benefit.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! A-levels are approved non-advanced education. Now I need to check a few more details about Alex's studies:

**Is Alex studying full-time?** 

Full-time means at least 12 hours per week of supervised study (lessons, lectures, tutorials, etc. - homework doesn't count toward this).

Also, I need to confirm:
- Is this education funded or arranged by an employer, or linked to a job offer?

For most A-level students at sixth form college, this is full-time education and not employer-funded, but I need to confirm this for Alex's situation.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he's studying full-time at the sixth form college - it's the usual A-level course with lessons during the week. And no, it's not funded by an employer or anything like that - just regular sixth form education.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's exactly the type of approved education that qualifies. A-levels studied full-time at sixth form college are non-advanced education with more than 12 hours per week of supervised study.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Now I need to check about Alex's work situation:

**Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week (or not in paid work at all)?**

Even if a young person is in approved education, they won't qualify for Child Benefit if they're working 24 hours or more per week in paid employment.

Does Alex have a part-time job, and if so, how many hours per week does he work?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, Alex doesn't work at all - he's just focused on his studies at the moment.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Alex is focused on his studies with no paid work, so that's fine.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to check:

**Is Alex receiving any benefits in his own right?**

Specifically, is he claiming:
- Employment and Support Allowance (ESA), or
- Universal Credit

in his own name?

If he's not claiming any benefits in his own right, that's fine for Child Benefit purposes.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I'm not sure about that - I don't know if he's claiming anything in his own name or not.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That's okay! Let me help clarify this. 

For an 18-year-old living at home and studying full-time A-levels, it would be quite unusual for them to be claiming Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) in their own right. These are benefits typically claimed by:

- People who are unable to work due to illness or disability (ESA)
- People on low income who are working, looking for work, or unable to work (Universal Credit)

Since Alex is studying full-time and not working, he's unlikely to be claiming these benefits. 

**To the best of your knowledge:**
- Has Alex made any benefit claims himself?
- Does he receive any disability-related benefits or support payments in his own name?

If you're not aware of him claiming any benefits himself, then the answer would be "no, he's not receiving these benefits in his own right," and we can continue with the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, as far as I know he hasn't made any benefit claims himself. I don't think he's receiving any benefits in his own name.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's fine then - if Alex hasn't made any benefit claims in his own name, we can continue.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to check:

**Is Alex doing an apprenticeship?**

You mentioned he's doing A-levels at sixth form college, which sounds like regular education rather than an apprenticeship. But I need to confirm - is he enrolled in any type of apprenticeship program (such as an English Apprenticeship, Scottish Modern Apprenticeship, or Welsh apprenticeship)?

Or is he purely studying A-levels without any apprenticeship element?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not doing an apprenticeship - just studying A-levels at sixth form, nothing to do with apprenticeships.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! That's clear - Alex is just doing regular A-levels, not an apprenticeship.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Now I need to check your residency status, as the claimant must meet UK residency requirements.

**Do you normally live in the UK?**

Most people will simply answer yes to this. However, if your situation is different, Child Benefit may still be available if you meet one of these special circumstances:
- You have settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme
- You're living abroad as a Crown servant
- Other qualifying situations

Do you normally live in the UK?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I live in the UK.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! You normally live in the UK, so that satisfies the residency requirement.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! Now I need to check about your responsibility for Alex.

**Are you responsible for Alex?**

You mentioned earlier that Alex lives at home with you. This means you satisfy the responsibility requirement because you live with him.

Just to confirm: Alex does live with you in your home, correct?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, that's right - Alex lives at home with me.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! You live with Alex, so you meet the responsibility requirement.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to check:

**Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex?**

Only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child at a time. For example:
- Is Alex's other parent claiming Child Benefit for him?
- Is anyone else (like another family member) claiming for Alex?

If no one else is claiming, or if someone is claiming but you've agreed between you that you should be the claimant instead, please let me know.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for Alex.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! No one else is claiming for Alex, so that's all clear.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Now I need to check Alex's living situation. You mentioned he lives at home with you, but I need to confirm there are no special circumstances:

**Is Alex currently:**
- In hospital?
- In local authority care?
- Being fostered?
- Or is he just living normally at home with you?

Based on what you've told me, it sounds like he's living normally at home, but I need to confirm this.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's just living normally at home with me - nothing like hospital or care or anything like that.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! Alex is living normally at home with you.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! Just one final check:

**Is the local council paying towards Alex's accommodation or maintenance?**

For example, is the council providing any payments or support for Alex's living costs or care?

Since Alex is living at home with you as a regular family arrangement, the answer is likely no, but I need to confirm this.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, the council isn't paying anything towards Alex - he just lives at home with me as part of the family.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent news! Based on all the information you've provided, let me navigate to the final outcome.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
## 🎉 Great News! You ARE Eligible for Child Benefit for Alex

Based on all the information you've provided, **you meet all the eligibility requirements** to claim Child Benefit for your son Alex.

### Why you're eligible:

✅ **Alex qualifies as a child** - He's 18 years old and in approved full-time education (A-levels)  
✅ **Approved education** - A-levels at sixth form college are non-advanced education with sufficient supervised study hours  
✅ **Not working excessively** - Alex isn't working 24+ hours per week  
✅ **Not receiving own benefits** - Alex isn't claiming ESA or Universal Credit in his own right  
✅ **Not in apprenticeship** - He's doing regular A-levels, not an apprenticeship  
✅ **You meet residency requirements** - You normally live in the UK  
✅ **You're responsible for Alex** - He lives at home with you  
✅ **No competing claim** - Nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for Alex  
✅ **Normal living arrangement** - The council isn't paying for Alex's care

### Next Steps:

1. **Apply for Child Benefit** - You can apply online or by post using form CH2
2. **Provide proof** - You'll need proof of identity for yourself and Alex, plus Alex's birth certificate
3. **Be aware of the High Income Child Benefit Charge** - If you or your partner earns over £60,000 per year, you may need to pay some or all of the benefit back through tax
4. **Payments** - Child Benefit is usually paid every 4 weeks

You can find more information and apply here: https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/how-to-claim

Is there anything else you'd like to know about claiming Child Benefit?

All eligibility criteria have been satisfied.
